properties.foundation_analysis: The underlying bedrock belongs to the Carboniferous Gullane and Wardie Formations of the Strathclyde Group, comprising interbedded sedimentary sandstone, siltstone, and mudstone sequences overlain by compacted Devensian glacial till. Structural masonry across the terraces is almost exclusively sourced from historical local quarries, dominated by Carboniferous Craigleith and Hailes sandstones—dense, quartz-arenite lithologies noted for low porosity, silty grain matrix, and pale buff to ash-grey hue. Subterranean foundation walls interface with natural sloping drainage towards the Water of Leith basin to the north. Structural mortar consists of traditional non-hydraulic and feebly hydraulic slaked lime (calcium hydroxide) mixed with well-graded local river sand, maintaining vapour-permeable interstitial jointing across all load-bearing ashlar courses.

properties.primary_surfacing: Engineered roadway and paved pedestrian curbs
properties.wear_characteristics: Authentic environmental patina and drainage grading

properties.botanical_analysis: Atholl Crescent Gardens and Coates Crescent Gardens feature mature urban broadleaf parkland landscaping. Identified species include mature European Lime (*Tilia x europaea*), London Plane (*Platanus x acerifolia*), Common Ash (*Fraxinus excelsior*), and Sycamore (*Acer pseudoplatanus*). Foliage is represented with dense, organic green leafy canopies, individual leaf cluster textures, and branching hardwood trunks, completely disambiguated from adjacent masonry.

properties.architectural_summary:
The scene captures the western gateway to Edinburgh's Georgian New Town along Shandwick Place (A8 corridor), flanked symmetrically by Thomas Bonnar’s Neo-Classical curved crescents: Atholl Crescent (southwest) and Coates Crescent (northeast), designed circa 1825. 
- **Atholl & Coates Crescents**: Continuous curved 3-storey plus basement and attic mansard/dormer residential palazzo blocks. Rectilinear, laser-straight floor plates with giant-order shallow Ionic pilasters anchoring the centre and terminal pavilions. Drop-front basement lightwells with perimeter wrought-iron spear-headed railings. Pitched timber roofs clad in Scotch/Welsh slate with repeating ridge-line ashlar chimney stacks and terracotta pots. Windows are strictly timber-framed 12-pane (six-over-six) sash-and-case fenestration.
- **St George's West Church (Shandwick Place)**: Designed by David Bryce (1866–1869), featuring a dominant 4-stage campanile-style clock tower (approx. 50 metres tall) with a rusticated stone base, pedimented clock tier, open columned belfry, and an octagonal pyramidal copper-clad spire.
- **Distant Landmarks**: To the northeast, the prominent drum and ribbed green copper dome of Robert Reid's West Register House (former St George's Church, Charlotte Square) terminates the lateral vista, with distant views across the Firth of Forth to the Fife coastline. All wobbly photogrammetric mesh artifacts are rectified into true vertical gravity planes, sharp pediments, and plumb street corners.
